newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says not yet talking with Russia on gas deal.
newsitem.headline: Japan says not yet talking with Russia on gas deal.

text.p: Japan said on Monday it was still staying clear of formal negotiations with Russia concerning a multinational, multi-billion dollar project that would develop potentially huge natural gas reserves in Irkutsk and transport supplies by pipeline to the Pacific.
"We have no intention of getting involved in the project at the current stage," a foreign ministry official said.
"We will see what we can do at the governmental level to get the project going after we see the results of the feasibility study," he added.

A Japanese business daily said on Monday that Japan had decided to hold government level talks with Russia on the project following Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's comments on Thursday that Japan hopes to dramatically improve its long-strained ties with Russia.

The project involves the development of the Kovyktinskoye gas field near Lake Baikal, which is estimated to possess recoverable gas reserves of 30 trillion cubic feet, and the construction of a pipeline that would run from the field through China, to South Korea and possibly to Japan.

State-run Japan National Oil Corp (JNOC) has been negotiating the project with Russia, China, and South Korea since last year, and is hoping to hold the first-ever meeting with the three countries in August.
The meeting, which has not yet been finalised, will discuss how the feasibility study should be carried out and how the study should be funded, a JNOC official said.
A meeting between the concerned parties had been tentatively planned for December 1996 in Moscow, but has met with repeated postponements.

Possible participants to the meeting include China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC), Korea Gas Corp, and Rusia Petroleum, which groups Siberia-Far East Oil Company (Sidanco), the state government of Irkutsk, a power utility in Irkutsk and South Korea's Hanbo Group.

Last month, Moscow signed a $7 billion deal with Beijing to supply China with 25 billion cubic metres (about 880 billion cubic feet) of natural gas a year from the Kovyktinskoye field over the next 30 years.
The deal may be eventually be incorporated into the possible gas field development and pipeline project to be carried out by the four countries, JNOC and the foreign ministry said.

Construction of the pipeline is estimated to cost from $4.5 billion to as much as $14.4 billion if it is extended to Japan's southern major island of Kyushu, a Sidanco official said last autumn in Tokyo.
Asian demand for natural gas, widely regarded as a cleaner source of energy compared to coal and oil, is expected to expand rapidly with the region's economic growth.
